'''Chilean literature''' refers to all written or [[literature|literary work]] produced in [[Chile]] or by Chilean writers. The literature of Chile is usually written in [[Spanish language|Spanish]].
Chile has a rich literary tradition and has been home to two [[Nobel Prize in Literature|Nobel prize]] winners, the poets [[Gabriela Mistral]] and [[Pablo Neruda]]. It has also seen three winners of the [[Miguel de Cervantes Prize]], considered one of the most important Spanish language literature prizes: the novelist, journalist and diplomat [[Jorge Edwards]] (1998), and the poets [[Gonzalo Rojas]] (2003) and [[Nicanor Parra]] (2011).<ref>[http://www.thisischile.cl/7297/2/chiles-nicanor-parra-wins-prestigious-cervantes-prize-for-literature/News.aspx Chile's Nicanor Parra wins prestigious Cervantes Prize for literature] www.thisischile.cl Thursday, December 01, 2011 retrieved September 17, 2013</ref>

'''[[Senegal]]ese literature''' is written or [[Literature|literary work]] (novels, poetry, plays and films) which has been produced by writers born in the West African state. Senegalese literary works are mostly written in [[French language|French]],<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Murphy|first=David|date=2008|title=Birth of a Nation? The Origins of Senegalese Literature in French|journal=Research in African Literatures|volume=39|issue=1|pages=48–69|doi=10.2979/RAL.2008.39.1.48|jstor=20109559|s2cid=161602141 }}</ref> the language of the colonial administration. However, there are many instances of works being written in [[Arabic]]<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal|last=Diallo|first=Ibrahima|date=2012-05-01|title=Qur'anic and Ajami literacies in pre-colonial West Africa|journal=Current Issues in Language Planning|volume=13|issue=2|pages=91–104|doi=10.1080/14664208.2012.687498|s2cid=145542397 }}</ref> and the native languages of [[Wolof language|Wolof]], [[Pulaar language|Pulaar]], [[Mandinka language|Mandinka]], [[Jola languages|Diola]], [[Soninke language|Soninke]] and [[Serer language|Serer]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite thesis|title=The Limits of the Literary: Senegalese Writers Between French, Wolof and World Literature|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/355567z3|publisher=UC Berkeley|date=2012|language=en|first=Tobias Dodge|last=Warner}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|title=The Pulaar book network: transnationalism from below?|url=http://mulosige.soas.ac.uk/the-pulaar-book-network-transnationalism-from-below/|last=admin_mulosige|date=2018-02-05|website=Mulosige|language=en-GB|access-date=2020-05-26}}</ref> [[Oral tradition]]s, in the form of [[Griot]] storytellers, constitute a historical element of the [[Senegal]]ese canon and have persisted as cultural custodians throughout the nation's history.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|last=Fall|first=Babacar|date=2003|title=Orality and Life Histories: Rethinking the Social and Political History of Senegal|journal=Africa Today|volume=50|issue=2|pages=55–65|doi=10.1353/at.2004.0008|jstor=4187572|s2cid=144954509 }}</ref> A form of proto-[[Senegal]]ese literature arose during the mid 19th century with the works of [[David Abe Boilat|David Abbé Boilat]], who produced written ethnographic literature which supported [[French colonial empire|French Colonial rule]].<ref name=":0" /> This genre of Senegalese literature continued to expand during the 1920s with the works of [[Bakary Diallo]] and [[Ahmadou Mapaté Diagne]].<ref name=":0" /> Earlier literary examples exist in the form of [[:Category:Islamic texts|Qur’anic texts]] which led to the growth of a form African linguistic expressionism using the [[Arabic alphabet]], known as ''[[Ajami script|Ajami]]''.<ref name=":1" /> Poets of this genre include [[Ahmad Ayan Sih]] and [[Dhu al-nunp|Dhu al-nun]].<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal|last1=Abdullah|first1=Abdul-Samad|last2=Abdullah|first2=Abdul-Sawad|date=2004|title=Arabic Poetry in West Africa: An Assessment of the Panegyric and Elegy Genres in Arabic Poetry of the 19th and 20th Centuries in Senegal and Nigeria|journal=Journal of Arabic Literature|volume=35|issue=3|pages=368–390|doi=10.1163/1570064042565302|jstor=4183524 }}</ref>[[File:LocationSenegal.png|thumb|[[Senegal]], located on the tip of [[West Africa]]|alt=|185x185px]][[File:DavidBoilat.png|thumb|[[David Abbé Boilat]]]]Post-colonial Senegalese work often includes emphasis on "national literature",<ref name=":0" /> a contemporary form of writing which stressed the engagement between language, national identity and literature. Senegalese novelists of this period include [[Cheikh Hamidou Kane]], [[Boubacar Boris Diop]] and [[Ousmane Sembène|Ousmane Sembene]]. Poets include former Senegalese president and philosopher [[Léopold Sédar Senghor]], [[Birago Diop]], [[Cheikh Aliou Ndao]] and [[Alioune Badara Bèye]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title=Senegal|url=https://aflit.arts.uwa.edu.au/CountrySenegalEN.html|website=aflit.arts.uwa.edu.au|access-date=2020-05-26}}</ref>

Female writers also contributed greatly to the body of [[Senegal]]ese works. [[Mariama Bâ]], [[Fatou Diome]], [[Ndèye Fatou Kane|Ndeye Fatou Kane]], [[Aminata Sow Fall]] and [[Fatou Ndiaye Sow|Fatou Sow]] have all written notable pieces regarding issues of [[polygamy]], [[feminism]] and the realities of Senegalese youth.<ref name=":5" />

[[File:Slab stele from tomb of Itjer at Giza 4th Dynasty c 2500 BC.jpg|thumb|upright=1.3|Slab [[stele]] from [[mastaba]] tomb of Itjer at [[Giza]]. [[4th Dynasty]], 2543–2435 BC. Itjer is seated at a table with slices of bread, shown vertical by convention. <!--Excavations 1903 by [[Ernesto Schiaparelli]], S. 1849. -->[[Museo Egizio|Egyptian Museum, Turin]].]]

[[Bread]] was central to the formation of early human societies. From the [[Fertile Crescent]], where [[wheat]] was [[domestication|domesticated]], [[Agriculture|cultivation]] spread north and west, to Europe and North Africa, and east toward East Asia. This in turn led to the formation of towns, which curtailed [[nomadic]] lifestyles, and gave rise to other forms of societal organization. Similar developments occurred in the Americas with maize and in Asia with rice.

It was one of the most highly contested [[New gTLD Program|new gTLDs]], with eight applicants in contention. On April 17, 2019, the .MUSIC registry, the [[International Federation of the Phonographic Industry]], [[Confédération Internationale des Sociétés d'Auteurs et Compositeurs]], the [[International Federation of Musicians]], the International Federation of Arts Councils and Culture Agencies, the [[Recording Industry Association of America]], the [[National Music Publishers' Association]], [[The Recording Academy]], the [[Independent Music Companies Association]], the Worldwide Independent Network, the [[American Association of Independent Music]], the NSAI, the [[National Association of Music Merchants]] (NAMM), and the Independent Music Publishers International Forum (IMPF) announced that the global music community based application, that was supported by a global music coalition with members representing over 95% of global music consumed, was approved by the [[Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers]] (ICANN).{{Cite web |url=http://music.us/press-releases/global-music-community-wins-music-domain-extension-rights/ |title=Global music community prevails in winning the rights to the .MUSIC domain extension |access-date=2021-03-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024000047/https://music.us/press-releases/global-music-community-wins-music-domain-extension-rights/ |archive-date=2020-10-24 }} The .MUSIC registry agreement was signed on May 4, 2021.{{Cite web |url=https://www.icann.org/en/registry-agreements/details/music?section=agreement |title=.music Registry Agreement |access-date=2021-09-20}}

{{Short description|Interstellar clouds of cosmic dust}}
[[File:Dark Rift 2012.jpg|thumb|upright=1.5|This [[exposure (photography)|overexposed]] photo shows just over half of the inward bulk of the [[Milky Way]] (including its centre). As in all real images from [[Orion Arm|our Arm]] of the galaxy, much is obscured by the Great Rift (dark [[cosmic dust|dust clouds]] that span from [[Cygnus (constellation)|Cygnus]] to [[Centaurus]]).]]

In [[astronomy]], the '''Great Rift''' (sometimes called the '''Dark Rift''' or less commonly the '''Dark River''') is a [[dust lane|dark band]] caused by [[interstellar cloud]]s of [[cosmic dust]] that significantly obscure ([[extinction (astronomy)|extinguish]]) the [[Galactic Center|center]] and most radial sectors of the [[Milky Way]] [[galaxy]] from [[Earth]]'s perspective.

In dark, clear [[night sky|night skies]], the rift appears as clear as the bright [[galactic bulge|bulge]] of stars around the Galactic Center does to the [[naked eye]] or [[binoculars]]. The rift is largely between the [[Solar System]] (which is close to the inner edge of the [[Orion Arm]]) and the next arm, inward, the [[Sagittarius Arm]]. The clouds are an obstruction to millions of the galaxy's stars detected at [[visible spectrum|visible wavelengths]], which compose a bright hazy band appearing [[angular diameter|30° wide]] and arching through the night sky. The clouds within our radial sector of the galaxy span about {{convert|800–1000|pc|ly|lk=on}} from Earth.<ref>{{cite journal |bibcode=2015ApJ...810...25G |doi=10.1088/0004-637X/810/1/25 |arxiv=1507.01005 |title=A Three-Dimensional Map of Milky Way Dust |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=810 |issue=1 |pages=25 |year=2015 |last1=Green |first1=Gregory M |last2=Schlafly |first2=Edward F |last3=Finkbeiner |first3=Douglas P |last4=Rix |first4=Hans-Walter |last5=Martin |first5=Nicolas |last6=Burgett |first6=William |last7=Draper |first7=Peter W |last8=Flewelling |first8=Heather |last9=Hodapp |first9=Klaus |last10=Kaiser |first10=Nicholas|last11=Kudritzki |first11=Rolf Peter |last12=Magnier |first12=Eugene |last13=Metcalfe |first13=Nigel |last14=Price |first14=Paul |last15=Tonry |first15=John |last16=Wainscoat |first16=Richard|s2cid=55653509 }}</ref> The clouds are estimated to contain about 1 million [[solar mass]]es of [[plasma (physics)|plasma]] and dust.<ref name="EarthSky">{{cite web |url=http://earthsky.org/clusters-nebulae-galaxies/the-great-rift-in-the-milky-way |title=Great Rift: Dark area in the Milky Way |year=2010 |publisher=[[Earth & Sky|EarthSky]] Communications |access-date=2010-06-15}}</ref>

Suppl. | ISSN3 = 0920-5632 | CODEN3 = NPBSE7 }} '''''Nuclear Physics A''''', '''''Nuclear Physics B''''', '''''Nuclear Physics B: Proceedings Supplements''''' and discontinued '''''Nuclear Physics''''' are [[peer-reviewed]] [[scientific journal]]s published by [[Elsevier]]. The scope of ''Nuclear Physics A'' is [[Nuclear physics|nuclear]] and [[hadron|hadronic physics]], and that of ''Nuclear Physics B'' is [[high energy physics]], [[quantum field theory]], [[statistical physics|statistical systems]], and [[mathematical physics]]. ''Nuclear Physics'' was established in 1956, and then split into ''Nuclear Physics A'' and ''Nuclear Physics B'' in 1967.{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/00295582 |title=Nuclear Physics |publisher=ScienceDirect.com |access-date=2015-02-17}} A supplement series to ''Nuclear Physics B'', called ''Nuclear Physics B: Proceedings Supplements'' has been published from 1987 onwards until 2015 and continues as ''Nuclear and Particle Physics Proceedings''.{{cite web|url=http://www.sciencedirect.com/science/journal/09205632 |title=Nuclear Physics B - Proceedings Supplements |publisher=ScienceDirect.com |date=2024-03-07 |access-date=2024-03-07}} ''Nuclear Physics B'' is part of the [[SCOAP3|SCOAP3]] initiative. {{cite web |title=SCOAP3 Journals: APCs and articles |url=http://scoap3.org/scoap3journals/journals-apc |publisher=[[SCOAP3|SCOAP3]] |access-date=2014-09-15 }}

Sodium ions ({{chem2|Na+}}) are necessary in small amounts for some types of [[plant]]s,<ref name=":0">
{{cite journal
|first1=Tsuyoshi
|last1=Furumoto
|date=24 Aug 2011
|volume=476
|issue=7361
|pages=472–475
|journal=Nature
|title=A plastidial sodium-dependent pyruvate transporter
|doi=10.1038/nature10250
|pmid=21866161
|bibcode=2011Natur.476..472F
|s2cid=205225645
|url=https://pub.uni-bielefeld.de/record/2915158
|url-access=subscription
}}
</ref> but [[sodium]] as a nutrient is more generally needed in larger amounts<ref name=":0" /> by [[animal]]s, due to their use of it for generation of [[nerve impulse]]s and for maintenance of [[electrolyte]] balance and [[fluid balance]]. In animals, sodium ions are necessary for the aforementioned functions and for [[heart]] activity and certain [[metabolism|metabolic]] functions.<ref>
{{cite book
|last1=Pohl
|first1=Hanna R.
|last2=Wheeler
|first2=John S.
|first3=H. Edward
|last3=Murray
|editor=Astrid Sigel, Helmut Sigel and Roland K. O. Sigel
|title=Interrelations between Essential Metal Ions and Human Diseases
|series=Metal Ions in Life Sciences
|volume=13
|year=2013
|publisher=Springer
|pages=29–47
|chapter=Chapter 2. Sodium and Potassium in Health and Disease
|doi=10.1007/978-94-007-7500-8_2
|pmid=24470088
|isbn=978-94-007-7499-5
}}</ref> The [[health effects of salt]] reflect what happens when the body has too much or too little sodium.
Characteristic concentrations of [[sodium]] in model organisms are: 10 [[molar concentration|mM]] in ''E. coli'', 30 mM in budding yeast, 10 mM in mammalian cell and 100 mM in blood plasma.<ref>{{cite web|url = http://book.bionumbers.org/what-are-the-concentrations-of-different-ions-in-cells/|title =Cell Biology by the Numbers: What are the concentrations of different ions in cells? |website =book.bionumbers.org|first1= Ron|last1= Milo|first2= Rob |last2=Philips|access-date=8 March 2017}}</ref>

Additionally, sodium ions are essential to several cellular processes. They are responsible for the co-transport of glucose in the sodium glucose symport, are used to help maintain membrane polarity with the help of the sodium potassium pump, and are paired with water to thin the mucus of the airway lumen when the active Cystic Fibrosis Transport Receptor moves chloride ions into the airway.<ref name=":1" />

{{short description|Attempts to unify relativity, gravitation, and quantum mechanics}}
{{DISPLAYTITLE:''cGh'' physics}}
{{multiple image
|image1  =cube_of_theoretical_physics.svg
|caption1=A depiction of the cGh cube
|image2  =Venn_diagram_of_theoretical_physics.svg
|caption2=Depicted as a Venn diagram
}}
[[File:Quantum gravity.svg|thumb|410px|Diagram showing where quantum gravity sits in the a near-cube hierarchy of physics theories. Note that [[electromagnetism]] and [[quantum field theory in curved spacetime]] are added in as an extra and distinct items.]]
'''''cGh'' physics''' refers to the historical attempts in physics to unify [[General relativity|relativity]], [[gravitation]], and [[quantum mechanics]], in particular following the ideas of [[Matvei Petrovich Bronstein]] and [[George Gamow]].<ref>{{cite book |last=Kragh |first=Helge |author-link=Helge Kragh |chapter=Relativistic Quantum Mechanics |date=2009 |chapter-url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/978-3-540-70626-7_184 |title=Compendium of Quantum Physics |pages=632–637 |editor-last=Greenberger |editor-first=Daniel |place=Berlin, Heidelberg |publisher=Springer |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-3-540-70626-7_184 |isbn=978-3-540-70622-9 |access-date=2022-03-23 |editor2-last=Hentschel |editor2-first=Klaus |editor3-last=Weinert |editor3-first=Friedel}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kragh |first=Helge |author-link=Helge Kragh |date=1995 |title=Review of Matvei Petrovich Bronstein and Soviet Theoretical Physics in the Thirties |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/235090 |journal=[[Isis (journal)|Isis]] |volume=86 |issue=3 |pages=520 |doi=10.1086/357307 |jstor=235090 |issn=0021-1753|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The letters are the standard symbols for the [[speed of light]] ({{mvar|c}}), the [[gravitational constant]] ({{mvar|G}}), and the [[Planck constant]] ({{mvar|h}}).

If one considers these three [[universal constant]]s as the basis for a 3-D coordinate system and envisions a cube, then this pedagogic construction provides a framework, which is referred to as the '''''cGh'' cube''', or '''physics cube''', or '''cube of theoretical physics''' ('''CTP''').<ref>{{Cite book |title=Sleeping Beauties in Theoretical Physics |last=Padmanabhan |first=Thanu |chapter=The Grand Cube of Theoretical Physics |publisher=Springer |year=2015 |pages=1–8 |isbn=978-3319134420 }}</ref> This cube can be used for organizing major subjects within physics as occupying each of the eight corners.<ref>{{cite book |first=Gennady E. |last=Gorelik |author-link=Gennady Gorelik |title=Studies in the History of General Relativity |chapter=First Steps of Quantum Gravity and the Planck Values |date=1992 |pages=364–379 |publisher=Birkhäuser |isbn=978-0-8176-3479-7 |chapter-url=http://people.bu.edu/gorelik/cGh_FirstSteps92_MPB_36/cGh_FirstSteps92_text.htm |access-date=2009-05-07 |archive-date=2019-04-25 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190425200045/http://people.bu.edu/gorelik/cGh_FirstSteps92_MPB_36/cGh_FirstSteps92_text.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Wainwright |first=C. J. |title=The Physics Cube |url=http://www.cjwainwright.co.uk/maths/physicscube/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120306041426/http://www.cjwainwright.co.uk/maths/physicscube/ |archive-date=6 March 2012}}</ref> The eight corners of the ''cGh'' physics cube are:
* [[Classical mechanics]] (_, _, _)
* [[Special relativity]] ({{mvar|c}}, _, _), [[gravitation]] (_, {{mvar|G}}, _), [[quantum mechanics]] (_, _, {{mvar|h}})
* [[General relativity]] ({{mvar|c}}, {{mvar|G}}, _), [[quantum field theory]] ({{mvar|c}}, _, {{mvar|h}}), non-relativistic quantum theory with gravity (_, {{mvar|G}}, {{mvar|h}})
* [[Theory of everything]], or relativistic [[quantum gravity]] ({{mvar|c}}, {{mvar|G}}, {{mvar|h}})

Other ''cGh'' physics topics include [[Hawking radiation]] and [[black-hole thermodynamics]].

While there are several other physical constants, these three are given special consideration because they can be used to define all Planck units and thus all physical quantities.<ref>{{cite journal| last = Duff | first = Michael |author2=Okun |author3=Veneziano| title= Trialogue on the number of fundamental constants| arxiv = physics/0110060| journal = [[Journal of High Energy Physics]] | issue = 3 | year = 2002 | volume = 2002 | page = 023 |bibcode = 2002JHEP...03..023D |doi = 10.1088/1126-6708/2002/03/023 | s2cid = 15806354 |first2=Lev B.|first3=Gabriele}}</ref> The three constants are therefore used sometimes as a framework for philosophical study and as one of [[pedagogical patterns]].<ref>{{cite journal| last =  Okun | first = Lev| date = 1991-01-01| title = The fundamental constants of physics| url = http://www.iop.org/EJ/abstract/0038-5670/34/9/A05 | journal =  [[Soviet Physics Uspekhi]] | issue =  9 | pages = 818–826| doi = 10.1070/PU1991v034n09ABEH002475 | volume = 34|bibcode = 1991SvPhU..34..818O | url-access = subscription }}</ref>

'''Organomanganese chemistry''' is the [[chemistry]] of [[organometallic compounds]] containing a [[carbon]] to [[manganese]] [[chemical bond]]. In a 2009 review, Cahiez et al. argued that as manganese is cheap and benign (only [[iron]] performs better in these aspects), organomanganese compounds have potential as chemical reagents, although currently they are not widely used as such despite extensive research.<ref name="Cahiez2009">{{cite journal|title=Chemistry of Organomanganese(II) Compounds|first1=Gerard|last1=Cahiez|first2=Christophe|last2=Duplais|first3=Julien|last3=Buendia|journal=[[Chem. Rev.]]|year=2009|volume=109 |issue=3 |pages=1434–1476 |doi=10.1021/cr800341a|pmid=19209933 }}</ref>

{{short description|In biology, any group of fish that stay together for social reasons}}

In biology, any group of [[fish]] that stay together for social reasons are '''shoaling''', and if the group is swimming in the same direction in a coordinated manner, they are '''schooling'''.<ref name="Pitcher 365"/> In common usage, the terms are sometimes used rather loosely.<ref name="Pitcher 365"/> About one quarter of fish species shoal all their lives, and about one half shoal for part of their lives.<ref>{{cite journal | last1 = Shaw | first1 = E | year = 1978 | title = Schooling fishes | journal = [[American Scientist]] | volume = 66 | issue = 2| pages = 166–175 | bibcode = 1978AmSci..66..166S }}</ref>

Fish derive many benefits from shoaling behaviour including defence against predators (through better predator detection and by diluting the chance of individual capture), enhanced [[foraging]] success, and higher success in finding a mate.

Fish benefit from schooling through increased [[hydrodynamic]] efficiency, meaning they move faster and expend less energy.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.mdpi.com/2313-7673/11/4/278|title=Hydrodynamic efficiency...|website=Mdpi.com|access-date=June 10, 2026}}</ref>

Fish use many traits to choose shoalmates. Generally they prefer larger shoals, shoalmates of their own species, shoalmates similar in size and appearance to themselves, healthy fish, and kin (when recognized). The oddity effect posits that any shoal member that stands out in appearance will be preferentially targeted by predators, thus homogenising shoals.

[[Image:Fronton Cambodge Musée Guimet 9972.jpg|thumb|270px|A scene of the Mahabharata in an [[Angkor Wat]] stone relief: Two [[asura]]s, the brothers Sunda and Upasunda, fight over the possession of the beautiful [[apsara]] [[Tilottama]]. Some ancient Cambodian local legends were influenced by the Hindu epics.]]
'''Cambodian literature''' ({{langx|km|អក្សរសាស្ត្រខ្មែរ}}, {{Transliteration|km|Âksârsastr Khmêr}} {{IPA|km|ʔaʔsɒːsah kʰmaɛ|}}), also '''Khmer literature''', has a very ancient origin. Like most [[Southeast Asia]]n national literatures its traditional [[Text corpus|corpus]] has two distinct aspects or levels: 
*The written literature, mostly restricted to the royal courts or the [[Buddhist monastery|Buddhist monasteries]].
*The [[oral literature]], which is based on local [[folklore]]. It is heavily influenced by [[Buddhism]], the predominant religion, as well as by the Hindu epics [[Ramayana]] and [[Mahabharata]].

'''Homogenization''' or '''homogenisation''' is any of several processes used to make a [[mixture]] of two mutually [[Solubility|non-soluble liquids]] the same throughout.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Brakeman |first=Rob |title=Homogenizing Process {{!}} Homogenization {{!}} Sonic Mixing Corp |url=https://www.sonicmixing.com/homogenization-process/ |access-date=2024-02-01 |website=Sonic Corporation |language=en-US}}</ref> This is achieved by turning one of the liquids into a state consisting of extremely small particles distributed uniformly throughout the other liquid. A typical example is the homogenization of [[milk]], wherein the milk [[Globules of fat|fat globules]] are reduced in size and [[Dispersion (chemistry)|dispersed]]<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=2021-08-06 |title=Why Is Milk Homogenized and What Are its Effects? {{!}} Dairy Nutrition |url=https://dairynutrition.ca/en/milk-quality/homogenization/why-milk-homogenized-and-what-are-its-effects |access-date=2024-02-01 |website=dairynutrition.ca |language=en}}</ref> uniformly through the rest of the milk.<ref name=Britannica_online>{{Citation

[[File:Micrograph of homogenization of collagen.jpg|thumb|In [[histopathology]], pathologic homogenization is seen as a loss of variations, such as of [[collagen]] in [[lichen sclerosus]] (pictured).]]
'''Homogenization''', in [[cell biology]] or [[molecular biology]], is a process whereby different fractions of a biological sample become equal in composition. It can be a disease sign in [[histopathology]], or an intentional process in research: A homogenized sample is equal in composition throughout, so that removing a fraction does not alter the overall molecular make-up of the sample remaining, and is identical to the fraction removed. Induced homogenization in biology is often followed by molecular extraction and various analytical techniques, including [[ELISA]] and western blot.<ref name="pmid22528111">{{cite book |vauthors=Schmidt SD, Nixon RA, Mathews PM | chapter = Tissue Processing Prior to Analysis of Alzheimer's Disease Associated Proteins and Metabolites, Including Aβ | title = Amyloid Proteins | volume = 849 | pages = 493–506 | year = 2012 | pmid = 22528111 | doi = 10.1007/978-1-61779-551-0_33 | series = Methods in Molecular Biology | isbn = 978-1-61779-550-3 }}</ref>

'''Organoantimony chemistry''' is the [[chemistry]] of [[chemical compound|compounds]] containing a [[carbon]] to [[antimony]] (Sb) [[chemical bond]]. {{Short description|Academic discipline that studies humanity's origins}}
'''Deep history''' is a term for the study of the distant past of the [[human]] species.<ref name=twsNYT18>PATRICIA COHEN, September 26, 2011, The New York Times, [https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/27/arts/deep-history-takes-humanity-back-to-its-origins.html?_r=0 History That’s Written in Beads as Well as in Words], Accessed January 16, 2016</ref> As an intellectual discipline, deep history encourages scholars in [[anthropology]], [[archaeology]], [[primatology]], [[genetics]] and [[linguistics]] to work together to write a common narrative about the beginnings of humans,<ref name=twsNYT18/> and to redress what they see as an imbalance among historians, who mostly concentrate on more recent periods.<ref>''[https://www.nytimes.com/2011/09/27/arts/deep-history-takes-humanity-back-to-its-origins.html History That’s Written in Beads as Well as in Words]''</ref> Deep history forms part of [[Big History]], and looks at the portion of [[deep time]] when humans existed, going further back than [[prehistory]], mainly based on archaeology and using a wider range of approaches.

Proponents of deep history argue for a definition of [[history]] that rests not upon the invention of [[writing]], but upon the evolution of [[anatomically modern humans]]. According to [[Daniel Lord Smail]], perhaps the most prominent advocate of deep history, the concept of prehistory is recast as an arbitrary boundary that limits the ''[[longue durée]]'' perspective of historians, and which rests upon assumptions that history follows a teleological path beginning with the origins of [[civilization]] in [[Ancient Mesopotamia]].<ref>Daniel Lord Smail, ''On Deep History and the Brain'' University of California Press, 2008</ref> For example, Smail suggests that advances in disciplines such as [[neurobiology]], [[neurophysiology]] and [[genetics]] mean that there are more possibilities for understanding the distant past, and offer opportunities to explain how events such as biological evolution, global environmental change, and patterns of the spread of disease have affected humanity today.<ref name=twsMedHistory>{{cite journal|pmc=2668893 | pages=318–319 | volume=53 | issue=2 | journal=Med Hist | title=Book Reviews: On deep history and the brain | year=2009 | author = Stephen T Casper }}; Review of book by: Daniel Lord Smail, ''On deep history and the brain'' published by Berkeley and London,  University of California Press,  2008, pp. xiv, 271, 978-0-520-25289-9, Accessed January 16, 2016</ref> Proponents of deep history generally do not acknowledge what they claim to be the traditional barrier between conventional history, generally based on written documentation such as ancient scrolls or hieroglyphs on pyramids, and unwritten prehistory, based on archaeology, in the human past.<ref>{{Cite book|title = The History Manifesto|last = Guldi, Armitage|first = Jo, David|publisher = Cambridge University Press|year = 2014|isbn = 978-1-107-43243-7|location = Cambridge|pages = 86}}</ref>

A review of Smail's book by [[Steven Mithen]], professor of [[Archaeology]] at the [[University of Reading]], is sympathetic to some parts of his thesis, but says  "Smail may not be as closely acquainted with the ongoing debates in prehistoric archaeology as he might be", and on Smail's critical description of historians: "I have to take Smail’s word for it that such historians still exist, as after more than a century of prehistoric archaeology they would be an astonishing throwback to another age".<ref>[[Mithen, Steven|Steven Mithen]], [http://www.lrb.co.uk/v30/n02/steven-mithen/when-we-were-nicer "When We Were Nicer"], a review of ''On Deep History and the Brain'' by Daniel Lord Smail, ''[[London Review of Books]]'', Vol. 30 No. 2, 24 January 2008, pages 24-25</ref>

'''Marine chemistry''', also known as '''ocean chemistry''' or '''chemical oceanography''', is the study of the chemical composition and processes of the world’s oceans, including the interactions between seawater, the atmosphere, the seafloor, and marine organisms.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Pilson |first=Michael E. Q. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/an-introduction-to-the-chemistry-of-the-sea/3F3142B6C163A06BF0AD513D82A3EF18 |title=An Introduction to the Chemistry of the Sea |date=2012 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-88707-6 |edition=2 |location=Cambridge |doi=10.1017/cbo9781139047203}}</ref> This field encompasses a wide range of topics, such as the cycling of elements like carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus, the behavior of trace metals, and the study of gases and nutrients in marine environments. Marine chemistry plays a crucial role in understanding global [[biogeochemical cycle]]s, [[Ocean current|ocean circulation]], and the effects of human activities, such as pollution and climate change, on oceanic systems.<ref name=":3" /> It is influenced by [[plate tectonics]] and [[seafloor spreading]], [[turbidity]], [[Ocean current|currents]], [[sediment]]s, [[pH]] levels, atmospheric constituents, metamorphic activity, and ecology.

The impact of human activity on the chemistry of the Earth's oceans has increased over time, with pollution from industry and various land-use practices significantly affecting the oceans. Moreover, increasing levels of [[Carbon dioxide in Earth's atmosphere|carbon dioxide in the Earth's atmosphere]] have led to [[ocean acidification]], which has negative effects on marine ecosystems. The international community has agreed that restoring the chemistry of the oceans is a priority, and efforts toward this goal are tracked as part of [[Sustainable Development Goal 14]].

Due to the interrelatedness of the ocean, chemical oceanographers frequently work on problems relevant to [[physical oceanography]], [[geology]] and [[geochemistry]], [[biology]] and [[biochemistry]], and [[atmospheric science]]. Many of them are investigating [[biogeochemical cycle]]s, and the [[marine carbon cycle]] in particular attracts significant interest due to its role in [[carbon sequestration]] and [[ocean acidification]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gillis |first=Justin |date=2012-03-02 |title=Pace of Ocean Acidification Has No Parallel in 300 Million Years, Paper Says |url=https://green.blogs.nytimes.com/2012/03/02/pace-of-ocean-acidification-has-no-parallel-in-300-million-years-paper-finds/ |access-date=2020-04-28 |website=Green Blog |language=en-US}}</ref> Other major topics of interest include [[analytical chemistry]] of the oceans, [[marine pollution]], and [[anthropogenic climate change]].

'''Organoruthenium chemistry''' is the [[chemistry]] of [[organometallic compounds]] containing a [[carbon]] to [[ruthenium]] [[chemical bond]]. Several organoruthenium [[catalyst]]s are of commercial interest<ref>''Synthesis of Organometallic Compounds: A Practical Guide'' Sanshiro Komiya Ed. S. Komiya, M. {{Short description|Home of many cradles of civilization}}
[[File:Ancient Orient.png|thumb|upright=1.1|Overview map of the ancient Near East]]
{{Ancient Near East topics}}
The '''ancient Near East''' was home to many [[Cradle of civilization|cradles of civilization]], spanning [[Mesopotamia|Ancient Mesopotamia]],<ref>{{cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lbmXsaTGNKUC&q=daily+life+in+ancient+mesopotamia+iran+iraq+turkey+syria&pg=PA11 |title=Daily Life In Ancient Mesopotamia |isbn=9780313294976 |access-date=28 February 2015|last1=Nemet-Nejat |first1=Karen Rhea |year=1998 |publisher=Greenwood Press }}</ref>{{Efn|Modern-day [[Iraq]] and northeastern [[Syria]], as well as parts of southeastern [[Turkey]] and southwestern [[Iran]].}} the [[Levant|ancient Levant]],{{Efn|Modern-day [[Syria]], [[Lebanon]], [[Palestine]], [[Jordan]], [[Israel]], and [[Cyprus]].}} [[ancient Egypt]], [[Elam|ancient Elam]], [[Anatolia|ancient Anatolia or Asia Minor]], the [[South Caucasus|ancient South Caucasus]] and [[Armenian highlands]],<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|url=https://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/35301/Armenian-Highland|title=Armenian Highland|date = August 28, 2017|encyclopedia = Encyclopædia Britannica }}</ref>{{Efn|All of modern-day [[Armenia]], in addition to the [[Eastern Anatolia Region|Turkish Eastern Anatolia Region]], northwestern [[Iran]], southern [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], and western [[Azerbaijan]].}} and [[Arabian Peninsula|ancient Northern Arabia]] (including [[Dilmun]]).{{Efn|Modern-day southern [[Iraq]], southeastern [[Jordan]], [[Kuwait]], and [[Bahrain]].}} It is generally not considered to include [[Pre-Islamic Arabia|Pre-Islamic Arabia as a whole]], the [[Berbers|ancient Berbers]], or [[Nubia|ancient Nubia]], though it is sometimes classified as encompassing [[History of Iran|ancient Iran]]{{Efn|[[Media (region)|Media]], [[Parthia]], and [[Persis]]}}, [[Ancient history of Cyprus|ancient Cyprus]], [[Ancient Carthage]], and the [[Aegean civilization]]{{Efn|The [[Minoan Civilization|Minoan]], [[Mycenaean Greece|Mycenaean]], and [[Cycladic Culture|Cycladic]] cultures}}. Due to their subject matter and scope, [[ancient Near East studies]] and [[Near Eastern archaeology]], including the subfields of [[Assyriology]], [[Egyptology]] and [[Hittitology]], are among the most prominent research fields in [[ancient history]]. Other fields include [[Classics]], [[Classical archaeology]], [[biblical studies]], [[biblical archaeology]], [[Jewish studies]], [[Christian studies]], [[Iranology]], [[Sinology]], and [[Indology]], some of which overlap with them. Historically, the [[Near East]] denoted an area roughly encompassing [[West Asia|central West Asia]] and [[Egypt]], having been focused on the lands between [[Greece]] in the west, [[Iran]] in the east, the [[Caucasus]] in the north, and [[Arabia]] in the south. It therefore largely corresponds with the central core area of the modern-day geopolitical concept of the [[Middle East]]. It was strongly influential on [[Christianity]], the later [[Islamic world]] and [[Islamic culture|civilization]], which [[Early Muslim conquests|conquered and absorbed its remannts]] with the exception of indigenous non Arabized  [[Jews]], [[Assyrians]], [[Mandaeans]], [[Syriac Arameans]] and [[Armenians]],  all of [[Hebrews|who]] [[Israelites|directly descend from it]], and moderately so on the later [[Western world]] and [[Western culture|civilization]] via the [[Aegean civilization]], the [[Orientalizing period]], the [[Greco-Persian wars]], the [[Hellenistic period]], the [[Roman empire|Roman]] and [[Byzantine Empire|Eastern Roman]] empires, and [[Christianity]], while being distinct from yet to some degree culturally related and ancestral to them.

The [[History of the Middle East|history of the ancient Near East]] opens with [[Sumer]]'s rise in the 4th millennium BC and spans the [[Bronze Age]] and [[Iron Age]]; its terminus is debated, variously set at the [[Achaemenid Empire]]'s founding in the 6th century BC, the [[Macedonian Empire]]'s founding in the 4th century BC, or the [[early Muslim conquests]]' onset in the 7th century AD.

It was within the ancient Near East that humans first practiced [[History of agriculture|intensive year-round agriculture]], which led to the rise of the [[List of ancient cities#Middle East|earliest dense urban settlements]] and the development of many now-familiar institutions of civilization, such as [[social stratification]], [[centralized government]] and [[empire]]s, and [[organized religion]] (see: [[Religions of the ancient Near East|ancient Near Eastern religions]]) and [[History of warfare|organized warfare]]. It also produced the first [[Writing system#Invention of writing|writing system]], the first [[History of the alphabet|alphabet]] (i.e., [[abjad]]), the first [[History of money|currency]], the first [[Legal history|legal codes]], and the [[invention of the wheel]], advances that founded [[History of astronomy|astronomy]] and [[History of mathematics|mathematics]].

During this period, the region's previously [[Stateless society|stateless societies]] largely transitioned to building [[State (polity)|states]], many of which gradually came to [[Imperialism|annex the territories of their neighbouring civilizations]]. This process continued until the entire ancient Near East was enveloped by [[Middle Eastern empires|militaristic empires]] that had emerged from their own lands to conquer and absorb a variety of [[Cultural history|cultures]] under the rule of a top-level government.

'''Organosodium chemistry''' is the [[chemistry]] of [[organometallic compounds]] containing a [[carbon]] to [[sodium]] [[chemical bond]].<ref>''Synthesis of Organometallic Compounds: A Practical Guide'' Sanshiro Komiya Ed. 1997</ref><ref>C. Elschenbroich, A. Salzer ''Organometallics : A Concise Introduction'' (2nd Ed) (1992) from Wiley-VCH: Weinheim. {{ISBN|3-527-28165-7}}</ref> The application of organosodium compounds in chemistry is limited in part due to competition from [[organolithium compound]]s, which are commercially available and exhibit more convenient reactivity.

The principal organosodium compound of commercial importance is [[sodium cyclopentadienide]]. [[Sodium tetraphenylborate]] can also be classified as an organosodium compound since in the solid state sodium is bound to the aryl groups.
 
Organometal bonds in group 1 are characterised by high [[chemical polarity|polarity]] with corresponding high [[nucleophilicity]] on carbon.  This polarity results from the disparate [[electronegativity]] of carbon (2.55) and that of [[lithium]] 0.98, [[sodium]] 0.93 [[potassium]] 0.82 [[rubidium]] 0.82 [[caesium]] 0.79). The [[carbanion]]ic nature of organosodium compounds can be minimized by [[resonance stabilization]], for example, Ph<sub>3</sub>CNa.  One consequence of the highly polarized Na-C bond is that simple organosodium compounds often exist as polymers that are poorly soluble in solvents.

'''Radioanalytical chemistry''' focuses on the analysis of sample for their [[radionuclide]] content.  Various methods are employed to purify and identify the [[radioelement]]  of interest through chemical methods and sample measurement techniques.

'''''Computers in Biology and Medicine''''' is a monthly [[peer-reviewed]] [[scientific journal]] established in 1970. It covers the intersection of [[biomedical engineering]], [[computational biology]], [[bioinformatics]], and [[computer science]]. The journal publishes research articles, reviews, tutorials, editorials, and letters. According to the ''[[Journal Citation Reports]]'', the journal has a 2022 [[impact factor]] of 7.7.<ref name=WoS>{{cite book |year=2023 |chapter=Computers in Biology and Medicine |title=2022 Journal Citation Reports |publisher=[[Clarivate]] |edition=Science |series=[[Web of Science]] |title-link=Journal Citation Reports}}</ref>
